subtitle: Reading literature: images and participles
words.intro: Every German town has a *Literaturhaus*, or at least a reading in the back of a bookshop. There is a glass of water, a lamp and an author. The audience is more than usually critical, and they’ve all read it.

grammar[0].fact: A literary German text uses the Präteritum throughout, and it sounds to the ear like a book. *Es war ihr, als hätte …* is pure literature: no one has ever said it at a bus stop. Learn to read it. You needn’t ever say it.

grammar[1].blocks[0].note: Literary verbs are often the shortest ones. It’s the sentence around them that grows.

grammar[1].blocks[1].note: You’ll find these on nearly every page of every novel.
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: The best-known opening in German is about a man waking up as an insect: *Als Gregor Samsa eines Morgens aus unruhigen Träumen erwachte …* You could read the rest. It’s on this site, with a glossary.
grammar[1].fact: The Leipzig book fair gives a prize in spring, and Frankfurt gives the *Deutscher Buchpreis* in autumn. Both make their winners’ sales jump, and both will start an argument. The best-seller lists also separate *Belletristik*, fine literature, from everything else, which has been a debate of its own for centuries.

document.intro: A real poem, *Vagabund*, in the writer’s own hand, from 1929. It’s in the old German script. Don’t try to read it all. Start near the bottom: *Mich wird man einst still begraben … Kein Kranz, kein Stein meinen Namen tragen.*
document.fact: Sepp Mahler spent years on the road, painting and writing, and he lived until 1975. Germans learned this handwriting at school until the 1940s, so a box of family letters can be a closed book to the grandchildren. There are volunteers who transcribe them.

reading.intro: Maya’s first small book has done quite well, and she has a reading at a bookshop in Leipzig. Frau Huber is in the front row, her bag on her knee. Maya reads the new opening of her novel. It’s about an old woman at a window. Nothing in it is true.
reading.photos[0].caption: Goethe und Schiller in Weimar: Sie blicken auf.
reading.fact: The German book price is fixed by law, so a novel costs the same in a village shop as on the internet. That’s a large part of why those shops still exist.
